citation.title: Inference in Spatial Experiments with Interference using the SpatialEffect Package
citation.venue: Journal of Agricultural, Biological, and Environmental Statistics

standing_assumptions:
(S1) Setting [Section 2.1, p. 141 (PDF p. 4)]. “Specifically, suppose that we have a set of intervention nodes indexed by $i = 1, ..., N$, and these nodes are arrayed as points in a spatial field, $\mathcal{X}$. Each point in this spatial field, $x \in \mathcal{X}$, equals a coordinate vector of length 2 (recording, e.g., longitude and latitude coordinates). For point interventions, the coordinates of an intervention node $i$ can be given by $x(i)$.” “For each intervention node, we have a binary random variable $Z_i \in \{0, 1\}$ that connotes whether, at node $i$, treatment is activated ($Z_i = 1$) or not ($Z_i = 0$). Denote the ordered vector of random treatment assignments as $\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1, ..., Z_N)'$, with support $\mathcal{Z}$. We define potential outcomes such that at each point $x \in \mathcal{X}$, we would have outcome $Y_x(\mathbf{z})$ when the treatment assignment is such that $\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}$, and these potential outcomes are defined for each $\mathbf{z} \in \mathcal{Z}$. We stress that outcomes are defined at all $x$ values in $\mathcal{X}$, not just at the $x(i)$ values, which makes the setting bipartite.” “The outcome that we observe at point $x$, labeled $Y_x$, is the potential outcome associated with the realized treatment assignment vector: $Y_x = \sum_{\mathbf{z} \in \mathcal{Z}} Y_x(\mathbf{z})\mathbf{1}(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z})$, where $\mathbf{1}(\cdot)$ is the indicator function.” “(i.e., we allow for effects to be nonlinear and heterogenous).” Points and polygons [p. 141]: “these intervention nodes could be points or polygons. Wang et al. (2022) show that the analysis is essentially the same, and so for illustration here we will focus on point interventions.”

(S2) Design [Section 2.1, p. 142 (PDF p. 5)]. “Our analysis focuses on randomized experiments for which the distribution of the treatment assignment vector, $\mathbf{Z}$, is known. Our inferential results are derived from the treatment assignment distribution. Extensions to observational studies would follow if the treatment assignment mechanism resembled the kind of Bernoulli process assumed in Wang et al. (2022).” [Section 2.2, p. 142] “$\alpha$ is the experimental design parameter that governs the distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$ (that is, the probabilities of different treatment assignment vectors), $\mathbf{z}_{-i}$ is a vector of treatment values at nodes other than node $i$, and $\mathcal{Z}_{-i}$ is the set of possible values that $\mathbf{Z}_{-i}$ can take. The design parameter, $\alpha$, is an abbreviated way of capturing a variety of factors that might affect the distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$. For example, it could index vectors of treatment assignment probabilities for the intervention nodes, where such probabilities would determine the level of treatment saturation. It could also index the correlation structure for the treatments, which would characterize potential restrictions (for example, stratification or clustering) on the profiles of possible treatment assignments.”

(S3) Marginalized outcomes and point effects [Section 2.2, p. 142 (PDF p. 5)]. “we rewrite the potential outcome at point $x$ as $Y_x(Z_i, \mathbf{Z}_{-i})$, where $\mathbf{Z}_{-i}$ is the treatment status of all the intervention nodes except for node $i$. To concentrate on the effect generated by node $i$, we hold node $i$ to treatment value $z$ and marginalize over this variation in $\mathbf{Z}_{-i}$ to define an “individualistic” average of potential outcomes at point $x$: $Y_{ix}(z;\alpha) = \mathrm{E}_{\mathbf{Z}_{-i}}\left[Y_x(z, \mathbf{Z}_{-i})\right] = \sum_{\mathbf{z}_{-i} \in \mathcal{Z}_{-i}} Y_x(z, \mathbf{z}_{-i})\Pr(\mathbf{Z}_{-i} = \mathbf{z}_{-i}; \alpha)$.” “This allows us to define the causal effect at point $x$ of intervening on node $i$, allowing other nodes to vary as they otherwise would under $\alpha$: $\tau_{ix}(\alpha) = Y_{ix}(1;\alpha) - Y_{ix}(0,\alpha)$.” (The comma in the last term is the paper's.)

(S4) Circle averages and the AMR [Section 2.2, p. 143 (PDF p. 6)]. “$\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{z}); d) = \frac{1}{|\{x : d_i(x) = d\}|}\int_{x : d_i(x) = d} Y_x(\mathbf{z})\,\mathrm{d}\zeta$, where $d_i(x) = ||x(i) - x||$ is some well-defined metric that defines whether point $x$ is within a specified distance from intervention node $i$, which is located at $x(i)$, and $\zeta$ is a suitable integration measure.” “$\mu_i(z; d, \alpha) = \mathrm{E}_{\mathbf{Z}_{-i}}[\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}(z, \mathbf{Z}_{-i}); d)]$ is the potential $d$-radius circle average around node $i$, given that node $i$ is assigned to treatment condition $z$ and marginalizing over possible assignments to other points.” “$\tau_i(d; \alpha) = \mu_i(1; d, \alpha) - \mu_i(0; d, \alpha)$, is the average of individualistic responses for points along the circle of radius $d$ around node $i$.” The AMR for distance $d$ is denoted $\tau(d;\alpha)$; its display is misprinted (P008-T14 gives it as printed and corrected): $\tau(d;\alpha) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\tau_i(d;\alpha)$.

(S5) Estimator [Section 2.3, pp. 143–144 (PDF pp. 6–7)]. “the preferred estimator for practical purposes is the Hajek estimator (Särndal et al. 1992, pp. 182-184), given by: $\widehat{\tau}_{HA}(d) = \frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i=1}^{N} Z_i\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}; d) - \frac{1}{N_0}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(1 - Z_i)\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}; d)$ where $N_1 = \sum_{i=1}^{N} Z_i$ and $N_0 = N - N_1$.” Here $\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}; d)$ is the circle average of the observed outcomes.

(S6) Hypotheses and the two inference methods [Section 2.3, p. 144 (PDF p. 7)]. “The sharp null hypothesis states that the interventions have no effects whatsoever, such that $Y_x(\mathbf{Z}) = Y_x(\mathbf{0})$ , in which case all unit-level effects are also zero and the AMR is zero. If one assumes that the sharp null hypothesis holds, then the randomization distribution of the AMR can be simulated by simply permuting treatment assignment, estimating the AMR under each of these permutations, and then collecting the resulting set of estimates (Imbens and Rubin 2015, Ch. 5). The resulting distribution is referred to as the null permutation distribution.” The weak null hypothesis is “that the AMR equals zero”. The second method “provides confidence intervals that combine a normal approximation with a nonparametric spatial heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent (spatial-HAC) standard error estimator as proposed by Conley (1999).”

(S7) Package conventions [Section 3, pp. 145–146 (PDF pp. 8–9)]. [p. 145] “Users can choose a set of points that form the edge of a circle of radius $d$, that form a circular band (“donut”) centered at radius $d$, or that form a sector centered at $d$ (“disk”), by altering the option cType. When ras_Z is provided, the distance will be calculated from the boundary of each polygon and we implement polygon intervention. Otherwise, it is calculated from the center of each intervention node and point intervention is implemented.” [p. 145] “For the asymptotic variance estimator, users need to specify a distance threshold (cutoff) beyond which interference dependence does not exist.” [p. 146] “For a specified error rate of $\delta$ (e.g., $\delta = 0.05$), it is the $\delta/2$ and $1-\delta/2$ percentiles of the sharp null distribution generated by permutation. At each distance $d$, the sharp null hypothesis of no effect is rejected if the AMR estimate is smaller than the $\delta/2$ percentile or larger than the $1 - \delta/2$ percentile.” [p. 146] “The SpatialEffectTest() function generates the null permutation distribution of the sum of the AMR estimates within the specified range.”

(S8) Toy example [Sections 4–5, pp. 146–150 (PDF pp. 9–13)]. “The toy example includes 4 intervention nodes in a spatial field where outcomes are recorded in a 4-by-4 raster (left plot of Fig. 2).” “We suppose Bernoulli random assignment of the nodes to treatment, in which case there are 16 ways treatment could be applied, all with equal probability.” [pp. 147–148] “we choose dVec to be a sequence from 0.1 to 2 with an interval length of 0.1. The cutoff point for the spatial HAC variance is set to be 0.4 and the number of permutations is set to be 1000.” Footnote 5 [p. 148]: “The number doesn't make any difference here as there are in total 6 assignments.” (The six assignments are those with two of the four nodes treated, as in the observed assignment.)

(S9) Points the paper leaves open, fixed here so that the targets are definite (these are conventions of this file, not statements of the paper). (i) The paper does not say how a “quantile” or “percentile” of a finite permutation distribution is computed. The staged implementations call R's quantile() with its default rule (type 7): for order statistics $x_{(1)} \le \dots \le x_{(n)}$ and $q \in [0,1]$, with $h = 1 + (n-1)q$, $j = \lfloor h \rfloor$ and $g = h - j$, $Q_7(q) = (1-g)x_{(j)} + g\,x_{(j+1)}$ (and $Q_7(1) = x_{(n)}$). The printed toy percentiles $\mp 7.97$ are reproduced by this rule and lie strictly inside the range of the six enumerated values. (ii) $Y_{ix}(z;\alpha)$ uses $Y_x(z, \mathbf{z}_{-i})$ for every $\mathbf{z}_{-i} \in \mathcal{Z}_{-i}$ and both $z \in \{0,1\}$; a statement below that uses it assumes potential outcomes are defined at each such argument (for instance on all of $\{0,1\}^N$). (iii) $\mathcal{Z}$ is finite, so every expectation over $\mathbf{Z}$ is a finite sum. For a finite set of outcome points with counting measure the circle average is the arithmetic mean over the points with $d_i(x) = d$; every example below is of this kind or has outcomes constant on the circles concerned. (iv) The paper has no numbered results, no appendix and no proofs; every target is an unnumbered statement or display, located by page.

Scope of the list. The paper is a tutorial with no numbered results and no proofs. Three of its eight headline claims contain mathematical statements and enter as headline targets: P008-H1 (the definition of the AMR and its circle-average identities, P008-T25), P008-H2 (the sharp and weak null hypotheses, P008-T26, and the attributed consistency and normality statement, P008-T28) and P008-H6 (the additive case of the attributed equivalence with a structural coefficient, P008-T27). P008-H3, P008-H4 and P008-H5 are a simulated illustration, an empirical estimate and its interpretation; P008-H7 and P008-H8 describe the method and the package. Twelve confirmed errors have corrections that change a mathematical statement, a formula or a constant and are targets: P008-N012 (Major; the reference law of the Uganda permutation test), P008-E002 (Moderate; the percentile rule and the toy example's rejection), P008-N002 (Moderate; the toy example's cutoff), P008-N016 (Moderate; the sum of AMR estimates read as a change in a probability), P008-E015 (Moderate; the bandwidth formula of the archived variance code), P008-E003 (Minor; 12.38 for 8.00), P008-E004 (Minor; the step 5/111 for 0.5/111), P008-E005 (Minor; the misprinted display of the AMR), P008-E007 (Minor; the band described as a set of intervention nodes), P008-N001 (Minor; the band as described and as implemented), P008-N004 (Minor; the scale of the effect function in Figure 2) and P008-N009 (Minor; what the estimate at distance 0 averages). P008-E015, P008-N001, P008-N004 and P008-N009 set a sentence or figure of the article against the staged package or vignette, which is a later snapshot than the release the article cites; they are listed because each rests on an exact formal example or derivation and its correction replaces a formula, a constant or the description of the set that is averaged, and each target says which premise is read from source code and lies outside what Lean can establish. canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 2.2, the description of the circular band (“donut”): “of intervention nodes”, corrected to “of outcome points”
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] “Another option that the SpatialEffect package offers is to define the circle average as points that are within a $k$-coordinate-wide bandwidth around points that are $d$ coordinate units from the intervention node; this latter specification defines a disc or circular band (or “donut”) of intervention nodes that are between $d - k$ and $d + k$ coordinate units from the intervention node. The quantity $\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{z}); d)$ is the average of points selected with the specified distance metric.”

[Corrected; Sol's smallest repair] Replace “of intervention nodes” by “of outcome points”: “... this latter specification defines a disc or circular band (or “donut”) of outcome points that are between $d - k$ and $d + k$ coordinate units from the intervention node.”

[Formal content] (a) For a node $i$, $d \ge 0$ and $k \ge 0$, the band is $B_i(d, k) = \{x \in \mathcal{X} : d - k \le d_i(x) \le d + k\}$, a set of points of the spatial field, at which the outcomes $Y_x(\mathbf{z})$ are defined (S1), and the band average is the average of $Y_x(\mathbf{z})$ over $x \in B_i(d,k)$ with respect to $\zeta$, as the edge average of (S4) is the average over $\{x \in \mathcal{X} : d_i(x) = d\}$. It is not the set $\{j \in \{1,\dots,N\} : d - k \le \|x(i) - x(j)\| \le d + k\}$ of intervention nodes. (b) The two are different objects: if $0 < d - k$ and $d + k < \min_{j \ne i}\|x(i) - x(j)\|$, the set of intervention nodes in (a) is empty.
canonical_claim.note: P008-E007 is rated an error, Minor: a wrong noun in the description of a set; the displayed integral, whose variable is $x$, fixes the meaning. The validator's check is a page check; its finding is that the domain of the circle average consists of outcome points $x$, not of the separately indexed intervention nodes $i$. Part (a) is definitional; (b) was added when this target was fixed, is immediate, and only records that the printed description cannot be what is averaged (in the toy example distinct nodes are at least 1.4295 apart). The other wording of the same sentence (“$k$-coordinate-wide”) belongs to P008-N001 and is in P008-T17 (a).

Ybards[, d] <- (Ybard_sums[, d] - Ybard_sums[, (d-1)]) / (Ybard_lens[, d] - Ybard_lens[, (d-1)]) }else{ Ybards[, d] <- Ybard ... } Here d is the position in dVec, and Ybard_sums[, d] and Ybard_lens[, d] are the sum and the number of nonmissing outcome cells in the buffer of radius dVec[d] about each polygon; the function has no band parameter $k$.

[Statement refuted] That the archived “donut” estimate at the grid radius $d_j$ is the average over a band symmetric about $d_j$.

Counterexample (the validator's; exact rational arithmetic; run through the unmodified staged function). Two intervention polygons, a treated one and a control one, far apart; dVec $= (2, 4)$. The nonmissing outcome cells near the treated polygon are four, at distances $0$, $19/8$, $27/8$, $35/8$ from the filled polygon, with outcomes $4$, $2$, $0$, $8$; the four corresponding cells near the control polygon have outcome $0$.
1. Buffer of radius 2 about the treated polygon: one cell, sum $4$. Buffer of radius 4: three cells, sum $4 + 2 + 0 = 6$.
2. The code's donut value at radius 4 is $(6 - 4)/(3 - 1) = 1$: the average over the cells at distances in $(2, 4]$.
3. The band symmetric about radius 4 of the same total width 2, $[3, 5]$, contains the cells at distances $27/8$ and $35/8$, with average $(0 + 8)/2 = 4$.
4. The control averages are $0$, so the AMR estimate at radius 4 is $1$ as implemented and $4$ for the centred band. (The full buffer of radius 4, the “disk”, has average $6/3 = 2$.)
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
The band of the article: P008-T15. All distances in this fixture are Euclidean distances in $\mathbb{R}^2$. For a nonempty closed filled polygon $P$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}^2$, define $\rho_P(x)=\inf_{p\in P}\|x-p\|_2$. If $C$ is the finite set of nonmissing outcome cells with centres $x_c$, then, for every radius $r\ge0$, its buffer is $B_P(r)=\{c\in C:\rho_P(x_c)\le r\}$, including cells with centres inside or on $P$. A cell is represented by its centre, and the average over a nonempty set $S\subseteq C$ is $|S|^{-1}\sum_{c\in S}Y_c$. Thus, for dVec $=(2,4)$, the implemented band at radius $4$ is $B_P(4)\setminus B_P(2)=\{c\in C:2<\rho_P(x_c)\le4\}$; the comparison band of the same total width $2$, centred at $4$, is $\{c\in C:3\le\rho_P(x_c)\le5\}$.

In the validator's fixture, the filled polygons are $P_0=[-1/8,1/8]\times[-1/8,1/8]$ and $P_1=P_0+(20,0)$. The nonmissing cells within distance $5$ of either polygon are eight, with centres $x_{ic}=(20i+s_c,0)$, for $i\in\{0,1\}$ and $c\in\{0,1,2,3\}$, with $(s_0,s_1,s_2,s_3)=(0,5/2,7/2,9/2)$. Any other nonmissing cell is at distance greater than $5$ from both polygons, so it lies in none of the buffers or bands used here, and $C$ may be taken to consist of these eight cells. These centres belong to a common raster of square cells of side $1/2$. At the observed assignment $(Z_0,Z_1)=(1,0)$, the outcomes are $(Y_{00},Y_{01},Y_{02},Y_{03})=(4,2,0,8)$ and $Y_{1c}=0$ for every $c$. The own-polygon distances $\rho_{P_i}(x_{ic})$ are $0,19/8,27/8,35/8$, respectively, and every cross-polygon distance $\rho_{P_i}(x_{jc})$ with $i\ne j$ exceeds $5$. There is one treated polygon and one control polygon, so the Hajek estimate is the treated region mean minus the control region mean. The centre cell's distance to the topological boundary $\partial P_i$ is $1/8$, whereas its distance to the filled polygon $P_i$ is $0$.

canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected wording; Sol's smallest repair] Replace “$k$-coordinate-wide bandwidth” by “distance tolerance $k$ around the circle of radius $d$”, and “sector centered at $d$ (“disk”)” by “full disk of radius $d$ around the intervention node (“disk”)”; the endpoints $d - k$ and $d + k$ are kept. “For the tested staged polygon-buffer implementation only, describe donut at index j>1 as the added cells between nested rasterized buffers of radii dVec[j−1] and dVec[j], with the first index using the full buffer; describe disk as the full buffer.”

[Formal content]
(a) [Geometry of the printed band.] Let $p \in \mathbb{R}^2$, $d > 0$, $k \ge 0$ and $C_d = \{q \in \mathbb{R}^2 : \|q - p\| = d\}$. For every $x \in \mathbb{R}^2$, $\inf_{q \in C_d}\|x - q\| = \left|\|x - p\| - d\right|$. Hence the set of points within distance $k$ of the circle is $\{x : \max(0, d - k) \le \|x - p\| \le d + k\}$; when $d \ge k$ its radial width is $(d + k) - (d - k) = 2k$, not $k$ (for $d = 4$, $k = 1$: the interval $[3, 5]$, of width 2).
(b) [What the archived code averages.] Let $B_{j-1} \subseteq B_j$ be finite sets of cells with $|B_j| > |B_{j-1}|$, $S_j = \sum_{x \in B_j} Y_x$ and $n_j = |B_j|$. Then $(S_j - S_{j-1})/(n_j - n_{j-1}) = \frac{1}{|B_j \setminus B_{j-1}|}\sum_{x \in B_j \setminus B_{j-1}} Y_x$. With $B_j$ the nonmissing cells of the buffer of radius $d_j$ about a polygon and $d_{j-1} < d_j$, the archived “donut” value at index $j > 1$ is therefore the average over the cells at buffer distance in $(d_{j-1}, d_j]$: a band of width $d_j - d_{j-1}$ whose outer edge is $d_j$ and whose radial midpoint is $(d_{j-1} + d_j)/2$, not a band symmetric about $d_j$. At index $j = 1$ it is the average over the whole buffer $B_1$ (for $d_1 = 0$: the polygon's own cells).

canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] [p. 146] “We construct a hypothetical effect function by mixing two gamma-distribution kernels. This yields a non-monotonic effect emanating from each intervention node, which is presented on the right plot of Fig. 2.” [Figure 2, right panel] vertical axis “Effect on Yx”, horizontal axis “Distance from intervention node”; the curve falls from about $1.63$ at distance $0.1$ to about $-0.55$ near distance $1.2$ and rises to about $-0.19$ at distance $2.0$. [Caption] “The plot on the right presents the non-monotonic effect function.” [Figure 4, right panel, “True AMR” against “Distance (d)”; caption] “The plot on the right shows the true AMR curve in the toy example.” The true AMR curve reaches about $-1.26$ near $d = 1.4$.

[Corrected; Sol's smallest repair] Relabel the vertical axis of the right panel of Figure 2 “Kernel $f(d)$” and replace the last sentence of the caption by: “The plot on the right presents the non-monotonic kernel $f(d)$; in the toy example, each treated node contributes $3f(d)$ to the outcome in a raster cell whose centroid is distance $d$ from that node.”

[Formal content] Kernel (staged vignette; not printed in the article): $f(r) = 2e^{-2r} - \frac{128}{3}r^4 e^{-4r}$ for $r \ge 0$ (the density of a gamma distribution with shape 1 and scale $1/2$ minus that of a gamma distribution with shape 5 and scale $1/4$). Toy outcomes with amplitude $a$: for raster cell $c$ with centroid at distance $r_{jc}$ from node $j$, $Y_c^{(a)}(\mathbf{z}) = Y_{0c} + a\sum_{j=1}^{4} z_j f(r_{jc})$, $\mathbf{z} \in \{0,1\}^4$.
(a) For every node $i$, cell $c$ and assignment $\mathbf{z}_{-i}$ of the other nodes, $Y_c^{(a)}(1, \mathbf{z}_{-i}) - Y_c^{(a)}(0, \mathbf{z}_{-i}) = a f(r_{ic})$; hence $\tau_{ic}(\alpha) = a f(r_{ic})$ for every design, and with nonnegative circle weights $w_{ic}(d)$, $\sum_c w_{ic}(d) = 1$, $\tau^{(a)}(d;\alpha) = \frac14\sum_{i=1}^{4}\sum_c w_{ic}(d)\, a f(r_{ic})$: the AMR is a convex average of values of $a f$, and $\tau^{(3)}(d;\alpha) = 3\tau^{(1)}(d;\alpha)$.
(b) $f(r) > -\frac{384}{437} > -1$ for every $r \ge 0$. (With $h(r) = \frac{128}{3}r^4 e^{-4r}$: $h'(r) = \frac{512}{3}r^3(1 - r)e^{-4r}$, so $0 \le h(r) \le h(1) = \frac{128}{3e^4}$; $e^4 > \sum_{k=0}^{6} 4^k/k! = 437/9$; hence $h(r) < 384/437$, and $2e^{-2r} > 0$.)
(c) By (a) and (b), with amplitude $a = 1$ the true AMR satisfies $\tau^{(1)}(d;\alpha) > -384/437 > -1$ at every $d$. A true AMR of about $-1.26$, as in Figure 4, is therefore impossible if the effect of a treated node is the function plotted in Figure 2; it is consistent with $a = 3$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 6, “the starting point at 0 corresponds to the area within the boundary of each village”: an exact example in which the zero-distance edge summary and the within-polygon summary differ
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] [p. 153] “We set the range of distance values to be between 0 kilometer and 20 kilometers. We consider the experiment as an example of polygon interventions. Therefore, the starting point at 0 corresponds to the area within the boundary of each village.” [p. 145] “When ras_Z is provided, the distance will be calculated from the boundary of each polygon and we implement polygon intervention.”

[What is computed; from the validator, for the archived 2024 implementation with the default cType = "edge"] At radius 0 the selected cells are the boundary cells of the rasterized polygon (the cells of the polygon that have a neighbouring cell, among the eight, outside it); interior cells are not selected.

[Claim refuted] That the value of the edge-based estimate at distance 0 is the contrast of the outcome averages over the area within the village polygons.

Counterexample (the validator's; integer and rational arithmetic). Raster of unit square cells covering $[0, 20] \times [0, 10]$ (20 columns, 10 rows; cell centres at half-integers). Polygons $P_T = [2, 7] \times [2, 7]$ (treated, $Z_T = 1$) and $P_C = [12, 17] \times [2, 7]$ (control, $Z_C = 0$). Outcome $1$ at the nine cells whose centres have both coordinates in $\{3.5, 4.5, 5.5\}$ and $0$ at the other 191 cells. Each polygon contains $25$ cell centres ($5 \times 5$); its boundary cells are the $16$ outer cells of that block and its interior cells the central $9$.
1. Edge summary at distance 0: all $16$ boundary cells of $P_T$ and all $16$ of $P_C$ have outcome $0$, so the contrast is $0/16 - 0/16 = 0$.
2. Within-polygon summary: the $25$ cells of $P_T$ sum to $9$ and those of $P_C$ to $0$, so the contrast is $9/25 - 0 = 9/25$.
3. As potential outcomes: $Y_x(z_T, z_C) = z_T$ at the nine central cells of $P_T$ and $0$ elsewhere, with $Z_T, Z_C$ independent Bernoulli(1/2). The boundary averages are $0$ under all four assignments, so the AMR of the edge summary at distance 0 is $0$; the within-polygon effects are $9/25$ for node $T$ and $0$ for node $C$, so the AMR of the within-polygon summary is $\tfrac12(9/25 + 0) = 9/50$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Sections 2.3, 3 and 5, the percentile rule for the sharp-null permutation test and the toy example's rejection at $\delta = 0.05$, as printed
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed. [p. 144] “For a two-way test of the sharp null hypothesis for a specific AMR value with an error rate of $\delta$, one can evaluate the estimated AMR relative to the $\delta/2$ and $1 - \delta/2$ quantiles of the null permutation distribution. (We use $\delta$ for the inferential error rate here so as not to confuse with $\alpha$, which is defined above to characterize the experimental design.) Such tests of the sharp null are approximately in exact finite samples, where the quality of the approximation depends the extent to the which the simulated permutations cover the full set of possible permutations. We can also use a permutation test to test linear functionals of the AMR, such as the mean or cumulative AMR within a range of distance values. To do so, one evaluates the estimated AMR functional value against the null permutation distribution of the functional values.” [p. 146] “For a specified error rate of $\delta$ (e.g., $\delta = 0.05$), it is the $\delta/2$ and $1-\delta/2$ percentiles of the sharp null distribution generated by permutation.” “At each distance $d$, the sharp null hypothesis of no effect is rejected if the AMR estimate is smaller than the $\delta/2$ percentile or larger than the $1 - \delta/2$ percentile.” [p. 148, footnote 5] “The number doesn't make any difference here as there are in total 6 assignments.” [p. 149] “The results suggest that the AMR estimates are marginally significant when $d$ is small, where the estimates are slightly larger than the .975 percentile of the sharp null permutation distribution and the red line on the bottom is close to be positive.” [pp. 149–150] “The 0.025 and .975 percentiles of the sharp null permutation distribution of the cumulative effect are $-7.97$ and $7.97$, respectively, while the actual cumulative effect is 12.38. Based on an error rate of $\delta = 0.05$, we would reject the sharp null hypothesis that there is no cumulative effect on the distance interval of $[0.1, 0.5]$.”

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 2.2: the average marginalized response and the two circle-average identities (“$\mu_i(z; d, \alpha)$ is simply the circle average of the $Y_{ix}(z;\alpha)$ values”; $\tau_i(d;\alpha)$ “is the circle average of the $\tau_{ix}(\alpha)$ values”), with the rule of Section 4 for computing $\tau_{ix}(\alpha)$ in the toy example
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, p. 142] “$Y_{ix}(z;\alpha) = \mathrm{E}_{\mathbf{Z}_{-i}}\left[Y_x(z, \mathbf{Z}_{-i})\right] = \sum_{\mathbf{z}_{-i} \in \mathcal{Z}_{-i}} Y_x(z, \mathbf{z}_{-i})\Pr(\mathbf{Z}_{-i} = \mathbf{z}_{-i}; \alpha)$”; “$\tau_{ix}(\alpha) = Y_{ix}(1;\alpha) - Y_{ix}(0,\alpha)$. This defines the effect on raster cell $x$ of switching node $i$ from no treatment to active treatment, averaging over possible treatment assignments to the nodes other than $i$.” [Printed, p. 143] “$\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{z}); d) = \frac{1}{|\{x : d_i(x) = d\}|}\int_{x : d_i(x) = d} Y_x(\mathbf{z})\,\mathrm{d}\zeta$”; “Then, $\mu_i(z; d, \alpha) = \mathrm{E}_{\mathbf{Z}_{-i}}[\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}(z, \mathbf{Z}_{-i}); d)]$ is the potential $d$-radius circle average around node $i$, given that node $i$ is assigned to treatment condition $z$ and marginalizing over possible assignments to other points. The quantity $\mu_i(z; d, \alpha)$ is simply the circle average of the $Y_{ix}(z;\alpha)$ values. Finally, $\tau_i(d;\alpha) = \mu_i(1; d, \alpha) - \mu_i(0; d, \alpha)$, is the average of individualistic responses for points along the circle of radius $d$ around node $i$. This is the circle average of the $\tau_{ix}(\alpha)$ values for outcome at distance $d$ from intervention node $i$.” “Working with these terms, our target quantity is the average marginalized response (AMR) for distance $d$, which is simply the average $d$-radius effect over the intervention nodes: $\tau(d;\alpha) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\tau_i(d;\alpha)\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[\bar{\mu}_i(1; d, \alpha) - \bar{\mu}_i(0; d, \alpha)\right]$.” (The display is misprinted; P008-T14.) [Printed, p. 146] “We suppose Bernoulli random assignment of the nodes to treatment, in which case there are 16 ways treatment could be applied, all with equal probability.” [Printed, p. 147] “This corresponds to the difference in mean potential outcomes when node $i$ is in treatment versus in control, where these means are taken with respect to the set of assignments in the assignment matrix ($\mathcal{Z}$ in the formal analysis). ... For example, to calculate $\tau_{1x}(\alpha)$, we take the average over outcome values in graphs where node 1 is treated and subtract from it the average over outcome values in graphs where node 1 is under control.”

[Formal content] Fix a node $i$ and $d$ such that the normalizing constant $|\{x : d_i(x) = d\}|$ (the $\zeta$-measure of the circle) is positive and finite, with $x \mapsto Y_x(z, \mathbf{z}_{-i})$ $\zeta$-integrable on the circle for each of the finitely many $(z, \mathbf{z}_{-i})$.
(a) $\mu_i(z; d, \alpha) = \frac{1}{|\{x : d_i(x) = d\}|}\int_{x : d_i(x) = d} Y_{ix}(z;\alpha)\,\mathrm{d}\zeta$ for $z \in \{0,1\}$.
(b) $\tau_i(d;\alpha) = \frac{1}{|\{x : d_i(x) = d\}|}\int_{x : d_i(x) = d} \tau_{ix}(\alpha)\,\mathrm{d}\zeta$, and hence $\tau(d;\alpha) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{|\{x : d_i(x) = d\}|}\int_{x : d_i(x) = d}\tau_{ix}(\alpha)\,\mathrm{d}\zeta$.
(c) [Toy design.] If $N = 4$ and $\mathbf{Z}$ is uniform on $\{0,1\}^4$ (sixteen assignments with equal probability), then for every node $i$ and point $x$, $Y_{ix}(z;\alpha) = \frac18\sum_{\mathbf{z} \in \{0,1\}^4 :\, z_i = z} Y_x(\mathbf{z})$, so $\tau_{ix}(\alpha)$ is the mean of $Y_x(\mathbf{z})$ over the eight assignments with $z_i = 1$ minus its mean over the eight assignments with $z_i = 0$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 2.3: under the sharp null hypothesis “all unit-level effects are also zero and the AMR is zero”; “The weak null is implied by the sharp null, but the reverse does not hold.”
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] “The sharp null hypothesis states that the interventions have no effects whatsoever, such that $Y_x(\mathbf{Z}) = Y_x(\mathbf{0})$ , in which case all unit-level effects are also zero and the AMR is zero.” “These intervals characterize uncertainty for the estimated AMR, and can be used to test the “weak null hypothesis” that the AMR equals zero. (The weak null is implied by the sharp null, but the reverse does not hold.)”

[Formal content] (a) If $Y_x(\mathbf{z}) = Y_x(\mathbf{0})$ for every $x \in \mathcal{X}$ and every assignment $\mathbf{z}$ at which potential outcomes are defined, then for every design $\alpha$: $\tau_{ix}(\alpha) = 0$ for all $i$ and $x$, $\tau_i(d;\alpha) = 0$ for all $i$ and $d$, and $\tau(d;\alpha) = 0$ for all $d$. (b) The converse fails: there are a spatial field, nodes, a design and potential outcomes with $\tau(d;\alpha) = 0$ for every $d$ and $Y_x(\mathbf{z}) \ne Y_x(\mathbf{0})$ for some $x$ and $\mathbf{z}$.

The paper gives no example for (b); one witness (not from the paper): $N = 1$, a field consisting of the node and two points $x_+, x_-$ at distance 1 from it, counting measure, $Y_{x_+}(1) = 1$, $Y_{x_-}(1) = -1$ and all other potential outcomes $0$, so that the circle average of the effects at $d = 1$ is $0$ and the effect at the node itself ($d = 0$) is $0$; $0$ and $1$ are the only distances at which this field has points. The claim that under the sharp null the randomization distribution “can be simulated by simply permuting treatment assignment” is addressed by P008-T2 (it holds when the law of permutations is the law of the design), and the decision rule by P008-T3 and P008-T4.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 1: “when effects are additive or homogenous, the AMR is equivalent to the “spillover” coefficient in a linear structural model” (attributed to Wang et al. 2022): the additive case
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] “Wang et al. (2022) show that when effects are additive or homogenous, the AMR is equivalent to the “spillover” coefficient in a linear structural model. The AMR retains a meaningful interpretation when effects are heterogenous or non-additive.”

[Formal content checked by the audit; the linear structural model is not written out in this paper] Suppose potential outcomes are defined for every $\mathbf{z} \in \{0,1\}^N$.
(a) [Additive effects.] If $Y_x(\mathbf{z}) = Y_x(\mathbf{0}) + \sum_{k=1}^{N} z_k g_k(x)$ for functions $g_k : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$, then for every design $\alpha$, every node $i$ and every $x \in \mathcal{X}$, $\tau_{ix}(\alpha) = g_i(x)$. Hence $\tau_i(d;\alpha)$ is the circle average of $g_i$ over $\{x : d_i(x) = d\}$ and $\tau(d;\alpha) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{|\{x : d_i(x) = d\}|}\int_{x : d_i(x) = d} g_i(x)\,\mathrm{d}\zeta$, whatever the design.
(b) [Additive and homogeneous effects.] If moreover $g_k(x) = g(d_k(x))$ for one function $g : [0, \infty) \to \mathbb{R}$ and all $k$, then $\tau_{ix}(\alpha) = g(d_i(x))$, and for every $d$ at which each node's circle has positive finite $\zeta$-measure, $\tau_i(d;\alpha) = g(d)$ for every $i$ and $\tau(d;\alpha) = g(d)$: the AMR at distance $d$ is the coefficient $g(d)$ of the structural model $Y_x(\mathbf{z}) = Y_x(\mathbf{0}) + \sum_k z_k g(d_k(x))$.

canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P008-H6 is a statement attributed to Wang et al. (2022), which is not staged; this paper has no numbered result and does not write out the linear structural model or define its “spillover” coefficient. The formal content is the additive case as the audit checked it, not a transcription: one fresh reader verified in the toy example that with additive effects $\tau_{ix}$ equals the additive effect of node $i$ (to machine precision), and the validator of P008-N004 gives the derivation of (a) (derivation.md, section 3). Part (b) is its immediate specialization. The paper says “additive or homogenous”; what homogeneity without additivity would mean is not stated here and is not covered. In the toy example outcomes are raster cell values, so the AMR is an average of $g$ at the distances of cell centroids and (a), not (b), applies (P008-T18 (a)). The second printed sentence is an interpretive remark and not a target.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 2.3: “under a set of mild regularity conditions, the Hajek estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal” (attributed to Wang et al. 2022)
canonical_claim.location: p. 144 (PDF p. 7); the estimator on pp. 143–144 (PDF pp. 6–7); p. 145 (PDF p. 8)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] “the preferred estimator for practical purposes is the Hajek estimator (Särndal et al. 1992, pp. 182-184), given by: $\widehat{\tau}_{HA}(d) = \frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i=1}^{N} Z_i\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}; d) - \frac{1}{N_0}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(1 - Z_i)\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}; d)$ where $N_1 = \sum_{i=1}^{N} Z_i$ and $N_0 = N - N_1$.” “Wang et al. (2022) show that under a set of mild regularity conditions, the Hajek estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal. Essentially, the conditions require the intervention nodes are separated from each other and there exists an upper bound on the number of nodes that interfere with each other.” [pp. 144–145] “Wang et al. (2022) describe conditions under which these intervals are asymptotically conservative with respect to type-I error.”

[Reading] For a sequence of experiments with $N \to \infty$ that satisfies the conditions of Wang et al. (2022), $\widehat{\tau}_{HA}(d) - \tau(d;\alpha) \to 0$ in probability and $\widehat{\tau}_{HA}(d) - \tau(d;\alpha)$, suitably standardized, converges in distribution to a standard normal law. The conditions are not listed in this paper beyond the sentence quoted (separated nodes; a bound on the number of nodes that interfere with each other) and the reference on p. 142 to “the kind of Bernoulli process assumed in Wang et al. (2022)”.

[Sufficient version derived by the audit; not the cited theorem] Fix $d$ and write $M_i(\mathbf{z}) = \mu_i(\mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{z}); d)$, $m_i(a) = \mu_i(a; d, \alpha)$ and $\tau_N = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}[m_i(1) - m_i(0)]$. Assume $Z_1, \dots, Z_N$ independent Bernoulli($p$) with a fixed $p \in (0,1)$; $|M_i(\mathbf{z})| \le H$ for all $i$, $\mathbf{z}$ and $N$; and a dependency graph for the pairs $(Z_i, M_i(\mathbf{Z}))$, $i = 1, \dots, N$, of maximum degree at most $D$ for all $N$ (collections of pairs that are not joined by an edge are independent). Then $\widehat{\tau}_{HA}(d) - \tau_N \to 0$ in probability as $N \to \infty$ (the estimator being given any fixed value when $N_1 = 0$ or $N_0 = 0$).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Standing assumptions (S1)–(S5): the spatial field $\mathcal{X}$, the nodes $x(i)$, the assignment $\mathbf{Z}$ with support $\mathcal{Z}$, potential outcomes $Y_x(\mathbf{z})$ (p. 141); $Y_{ix}(z;\alpha)$ and $\tau_{ix}(\alpha)$ (p. 142); $d_i(x)$, $\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{z}); d)$, $\mu_i(z; d, \alpha)$, $\tau_i(d;\alpha)$, $\tau(d;\alpha)$ (p. 143); $\widehat{\tau}_{HA}(d)$, $N_1$, $N_0$ (p. 144). The conditions of Wang et al. (2022) are not stated in this paper and that paper is not staged. Dependency graph: a graph on $\{1,\dots,N\}$ such that any two disjoint sets of vertices with no edge between them index independent collections of the pairs $(Z_i, M_i(\mathbf{Z}))$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: The paper contains no proof (it has no appendix) and the cited paper is not staged, so no finite lemma of the cited proof can be located. The exact finite-sample facts on which the audit's sufficient derivation rests (validate/P008-E001/adjudicate/artifact/adjudication.md, sections 2 and 7), with $U = N_1/N$, $S_1 = N^{-1}\sum_i Z_i M_i(\mathbf{Z})$, $S_0 = N^{-1}\sum_i (1 - Z_i) M_i(\mathbf{Z})$, $r_a = N^{-1}\sum_i m_i(a)$: (i) for independent assignments with $\Pr(Z_i = 1) = p_i \in (0,1)$, $\mathrm{E}[Z_i M_i(\mathbf{Z})] = p_i m_i(1)$ and $\mathrm{E}[(1 - Z_i) M_i(\mathbf{Z})] = (1 - p_i) m_i(0)$; hence with common $p$, $\mathrm{E}S_1 = p r_1$ and $\mathrm{E}S_0 = (1 - p) r_0$; (ii) $\mathrm{E}U = p$ and $\mathrm{Var}(U) = p(1 - p)/N$; (iii) for $V_i = Z_i M_i(\mathbf{Z})$ or $V_i = (1 - Z_i) M_i(\mathbf{Z})$, $\mathrm{Var}\left(N^{-1}\sum_i V_i\right) \le H^2(D + 1)/N$; (iv) on the event $\{U \ge p/2,\ 1 - U \ge (1 - p)/2\}$, whose complement has probability at most $4p(1 - p)/(N\min(p, 1 - p)^2)$: $\left|S_1/U - r_1\right| \le \frac{2}{p}\{|S_1 - p r_1| + H|U - p|\}$ and $\left|S_0/(1 - U) - r_0\right| \le \frac{2}{1 - p}\{|S_0 - (1 - p) r_0| + H|U - p|\}$; and $\widehat{\tau}_{HA}(d) - \tau_N = (S_1/U - r_1) - (S_0/(1 - U) - r_0)$ when $0 < U < 1$. For the linearization and its covariances under additive outcomes and Bernoulli(1/2): P008-T6 (c).
canonical_claim.note: The asymptotic part of headline claim P008-H2. It is attributed to the companion paper, whose proofs the audit did not check (a recorded coverage gap); a formalization must not supply hypotheses in the paper's name. What the audit established, in the adjudication of P008-E001 (not confirmed as an error, since the sentence imports the full conditions of the cited theorem): the two properties named in the sentence are not by themselves sufficient for every design (exact examples: dependent assignment within pairs gives AMR $3/5$ and probability limit $21/25$; independent assignment with probabilities $2/3$ and $1/3$ and no effects gives AMR $0$ and limit $1/3$), and independent assignment with a common probability together with bounded outcomes and bounded dependence is sufficient for consistency (the version stated above). Asymptotic normality and the conservativeness of the intervals were not derived in general by the audit (the adjudication gives one nondegenerate normality witness) and are recorded here as printed only. The exact finite-sample statements of the same headline claim are P008-T26; the findings that touch the two inference methods are P008-E002 and P008-N002.
